newsitem.title: USA: Clinton opens drive for approval of chemical pact.
newsitem.headline: Clinton opens drive for approval of chemical pact.

text.p: With help from several top Republicans and a phalanx of military leaders, President Bill Clinton on Friday launched a drive for Senate approval of a treaty banning chemical weapons by an April 29 deadline.

Speaking at an outdoor ceremony that had all the trappings of a campaign rally, Clinton said the four-year-old Chemical Weapons Convention provided "clear and overwhelming benefits," and that swift approval was essential.
"If the Senate fails to ratify the convention before it enters into force, our national security -- and I might add, our economic security -- will suffer," he said.

Ratification is being held up by Senate Republicans and one of its key opponents, Foreign Relations Committee chairman Jesse Helms, later reiterated his determination to block the treaty unless the administration addressed his concerns.

Clinton said the United States would be unable to enforce rules that it helped write and that export-dependent U.S. chemical companies will face trade restrictions "that could cost them hundreds of millions of dollars in sales."

Joining the Democratic president at the White House rally on a warm and sunny spring day were James Baker, secretary of state under Republican President George Bush, former Kansas Republican Sen. Nancy Kassebaum-Baker and an array of other dignitaries, including retired Gen. Colin Powell and members of the Joint Chiefs of Staff that Powell once led.

Baker noted that the treaty had been negotiated under Bush and former Republican President Ronald Reagan, and said it was "outrageous" to suggest either of them would act against the best interests of the United States.

"If we fail to ratify the Chemical Weapons Convention, we will be sending a clear signal of retreat from international leadership both to our allies and our enemies alike. This is a message we should never, never send," Baker said.

The treaty was signed by the United States and 129 other countries in Paris on January 12, 1993. Although at last count 161 countries had signed and about 70 ratified the treaty, it has languished in the U.S. Senate since 1993.
If the Senate fails to approve it by April 29, the United States will lose the right to be regarded as a charter signatory, which backers say would severely restrict the U.S. role in enforcing it.

Opponents -- predominantly conservative senators but including at least four moderate Republican former defence secretaries -- say inspection provisions of the treaty are flawed and that states that are chemical weapons threats like North Korea, Libya and Iraq would not be bound by the pact.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said "this is like saying that we should not pass a law against drug smuggling because we cannot assume full compliance by drug traffickers."
Clinton said if the pact were not approved, "America will go from leading the world to joining the company of pariah nations the Chemical Weapons Treaty seeks to isolate."
White House spokesman Mike McCurry characterised Clinton's chances of winning approval of the treaty by the April 29 deadline as "uphill, but not too steep."
Helms, appearing in North Carolina with Albright on March 25, said he and the administration had been negotiating over the treaty and had managed to resolve a number of differences.
But after Clinton's appeal on Friday, Helms reiterated his opposition, which he said was shared by more than 50 generals, admirals and senior foreign policy leaders.

Helms, who has the power to stop the treaty from getting a full Senate vote, attacked the administration in a statement, saying if it "continues to stonewall... their opposition to making essential changes will ensure that the Senate never ratifies the CWC."
